sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll master Claude Projects — Anthropic's persistent workspace feature — including how to write instructions that dramatically improve Claude's behaviour, how to upload and organise files as a knowledge base, how different Projects serve different areas of your life, and the advanced instruction-writing techniques that professional Claude users use. By the end you'll have a fully configured Project for this course that saves you 10+ minutes every week.

## The Core Problem Projects Solve

By default, every Claude conversation is a fresh start. Close the tab and Claude has no memory of what you discussed. Open a new chat and you're explaining your context from scratch — again.

This friction compounds. If you use Claude daily, you might spend 2-3 minutes at the start of every conversation re-establishing who you are, what you're working on, and what you want. That's 10-15 minutes per day, just on context-setting.

**Claude Projects eliminate this.** A Project is a persistent workspace where:
- **Custom instructions** you write are automatically sent to Claude before every conversation in that Project
- **Uploaded files** (documents, code, PDFs, notes) are available as knowledge Claude can reference throughout all Project conversations
- **Conversation history** within the Project is retained — you can scroll back through all past chats
- **Consistency** is enforced — the same persona, tone, and constraints apply every time

Think of it as giving Claude a permanent briefing that it reads before talking to you — every single time, automatically.

## Writing Excellent Project Instructions

The instruction field is the most powerful part of a Project. Everything you write here shapes every conversation — so invest time getting it right.

**The 6 elements of strong Project instructions:**

**1. Who you are (1-3 sentences):**
```
I'm a UX designer at a mid-size software company. I primarily work on mobile
app interfaces. I have 4 years of design experience and some basic HTML/CSS knowledge.
```

**2. What you're working on:**
```
Currently focused on: redesigning our onboarding flow for new users and preparing
a presentation for our product roadmap review in Q3.
```

**3. Preferred response format:**
```
Preferences:
- Use bullet points for lists, not numbered lists (easier to add items)
- Keep responses to 3-5 paragraphs unless I ask for more
- When I ask a yes/no question, answer it first, then explain
- Use plain English — avoid UX jargon unless I use it first
```

**4. What to avoid:**
```
Do not:
- Suggest solutions that require a development team of more than 2 people
- Add lengthy disclaimers or caveats at the end of every response
- Recommend tools we don't already use (Figma, Linear, Slack, Notion)
- Use phrases like 'Great question!' or 'Certainly!'
```

**5. Domain knowledge to assume:**
```
Assume I know:
- Basic design principles (hierarchy, contrast, affordance)
- How mobile app development timelines work
- Our product is a B2B SaaS tool for project managers
```

**6. Default tasks or modes:**
```
When I paste a design critique or user feedback, your first response should always:
1. Summarise the key issues in 3 bullets
2. Rate overall severity (Minor / Moderate / Significant)
3. Suggest one quick win and one bigger fix
```

You don't need all 6 elements at once. Start with the most important and add over time.

## Uploading Files: Building a Knowledge Base

Files you upload to a Project become knowledge Claude can reference in any conversation — without you pasting them in again. This is especially powerful for reference materials you return to repeatedly.

**What to upload:**

| File type | Examples | Why it's powerful |
|-----------|----------|-------------------|
| Style guides | Brand voice document, writing standards | Claude applies your actual standards automatically |
| Reference docs | Technical specs, API docs, company overview | Ask questions about your specific docs, not generic info |
| Personal context | Bio, CV, goals document | Claude knows your background without re-explaining |
| Templates | Your report format, email templates | Claude follows your actual format, not its defaults |
| Rules | Privacy policy, AI rules from lesson 1-5 | Constraints enforced in every conversation |
| Active projects | Current draft, code file, data file | Claude can read, improve, analyse without repasting |

**Supported file types:** PDF, TXT, MD, CSV, DOCX, Python, JavaScript, and most common code files. Images work too.

**File limit:** Projects support up to 200,000 tokens of uploaded content across all files (roughly 150,000 words or 500 pages). Most users hit this limit only with very large codebases or many long documents.

**Referencing files explicitly:** You can ask Claude to use a specific file:
```
Using the brand voice guide I've uploaded, rewrite this marketing copy.
Using my CV, help me tailor my experience to this job posting.
Based on the technical spec I've attached, generate acceptance test cases.
```

Or you can let Claude reference files implicitly — when you ask about a topic covered in your uploaded files, Claude will draw from them automatically.

## Designing a Multi-Project System

Different parts of your work and life need different contexts. Professional Claude users maintain 3-6 Projects with distinct configurations:

**Work Project — your primary professional workspace:**
- Instructions: your role, company context, current priorities
- Files: company style guide, org chart, current project specs
- Use for: all work tasks, drafts, analysis

**Personal learning Project — for this course and future learning:**
- Instructions: your background, what you want to learn, how you learn best
- Files: your notes, prompt library, AI rules file
- Use for: course exercises, research, learning new topics

**Writing Project — for any substantial writing project:**
- Instructions: the project's style, audience, what you've decided so far
- Files: research notes, existing draft, style reference
- Use for: drafting, editing, consistency checking

**Technical Project — for coding and technical tasks:**
- Instructions: your tech stack, coding standards, your experience level
- Files: key code files, architecture docs, requirements
- Use for: code review, debugging, architecture decisions

**The key principle:** Different Projects = different Claudes. The Project instructions and files create a context-specific AI assistant calibrated to exactly your needs for that area of work.

**The fastest improvement you can make:** Add one "avoid" instruction to your Project. Think about the Claude response you find most annoying or least useful — long disclaimers? Generic caveats? Opening with 'Certainly!'? Add 'Do not [that thing]' to your instructions. You'll never see it again.

## Claude's Cross-Conversation Memory (Launched 2025)

Projects are a deliberate workspace you set up. Claude also has a separate **memory** feature — a system that automatically learns and stores facts about you across all conversations, not just within a specific Project.

**How it works:**
- As you use Claude, it identifies persistent facts worth remembering: your role, preferences, ongoing projects, communication style
- These are stored as memory entries you can view and manage in Settings → Memory
- Memory is injected into all future conversations automatically — Claude knows who you are before you explain anything
- You can also ask Claude to remember something explicitly: *"Remember that I work in healthcare and GDPR applies to everything I do."*
- You can delete, edit, or clear any stored memory at any time

**Memory vs. Projects — what's the difference:**

| Feature | Projects | Memory |
|---------|----------|--------|
| Scope | Conversations within that Project | All Claude conversations |
| How set up | You write the instructions manually | Claude learns automatically + you can add explicitly |
| Best for | Context specific to one domain or project | Universal preferences and persistent identity |
| Control | Fully manual | You review and edit what Claude stored |

**Practical use:** Memory means you don't have to explain who you are every time you start a new conversation outside of a Project. Projects give you deeper, domain-specific context within a workspace. Used together, they eliminate nearly all context-repetition overhead.

**To configure your memory:**
Start a conversation and say: *"I want to set up my memory. Please remember the following about me:"* then describe your role, preferences, ongoing work, and any constraints. Claude will store this and apply it to future conversations.

## Advanced: The System Prompt Layer in Projects

When you write Project instructions, you're essentially writing a system prompt — the invisible first layer of every conversation that shapes all subsequent responses.

Professional instruction writers use some specific techniques:

**The "I am" framing:** Describe yourself clearly so Claude calibrates to your level.
```
I am a non-technical marketing manager. I understand business concepts but
not programming. Explain technical topics in business terms.
```

**The task type trigger:** Tell Claude to behave differently for different task types.
```
When I send you a URL, summarise the page in 5 bullets before answering any questions.
When I paste a document, first identify its type and purpose before working on it.
When I ask 'what do you think?', give me your honest opinion, not a balanced both-sides response.
```

**The quality gate:** Set an explicit quality standard.
```
Before completing any writing task, review your output for: (1) jargon I didn't use
first, (2) vague claims without specific examples, (3) conclusions that don't follow
from the evidence. Fix any you find before responding.
```

**The expertise signal:** Tell Claude what you do and don't need explained.
```
Assume I understand: marketing analytics, A/B testing, and SaaS metrics.
Do not explain these unless I specifically ask. Do explain: technical concepts
above basic HTML/CSS level, legal or accounting concepts.
```

sections.title: Build Your Full Course Project
sections.content:
You'll create a fully configured Claude Project for this course. This will serve as your home base for every lesson from here on.

**Step 1 — Create the Project**
In [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai), find **Projects** in the left sidebar. Click **New Project**. Name it: `AI Course Learning`.

**Step 2 — Write rich Project Instructions**

Open the instruction editor and write your version of this template:
```
I'm working through an AI skills course. Here's my context:

Background: [2-3 sentences about your work/study background]
AI experience: [Complete beginner / Some experience / Intermediate]
Primary goals: [What you want to get from this course]

Preferences:
- Give practical examples alongside theory
- Define technical jargon when you use it
- [Add 2-3 more preferences that matter to you]

Do not:
- Open with 'Great question!' or 'Certainly!'
- Add lengthy caveats unless I specifically ask for them
- [Add 1-2 behaviours you want to avoid]

When I say 'explain that differently': try a completely different analogy.
When I say 'practical?': give me one specific action I can take today.
When I paste code: review it for correctness before anything else.
```

Personalise every section. The more specific you are to your real situation, the more useful the Project will be.

**Step 3 — Upload your files**
- Upload the `my-ai-rules.md` file you created in lesson 1-5
  *(Skipped lesson 1-5? Take 5 minutes now: open a text file, write 3–5 rules about how you want Claude to respond — e.g. "Be concise", "Don't add disclaimers", "Use British English". Save it as `my-ai-rules.md`.)*
- Upload your `my-prompt-library.md` if you've created it (lesson 3-8)
- Upload any personal context document: a brief bio, your work role description, or your goals for using AI

**Step 4 — Test your instructions**

Start a new conversation inside the Project. Ask:
```
I'm confused about the difference between few-shot and zero-shot prompting.
Can you explain it?
```

Does Claude's response reflect your instructions? Is it calibrated to your background? If not, edit the instructions and try again.

Then ask:
```
What should I focus on first after completing this course's foundations?
```

Evaluate: does Claude know enough about you to give a personalised answer?

**Step 5 — Create a second Project**

Create one more Project for a real area of your work or life. Write instructions appropriate to that context. This gives you 2 Projects to switch between — your learning Project and your real-work Project.

**Save a record:** In your notes or prompt library, copy the final version of your Project instructions. If you need to recreate the Project or share it with someone, you'll have the instructions ready.

sections.question: You set up a Claude Project with detailed instructions and upload your company style guide. Three months later, the style guide is updated. What do you need to do?
options: Nothing — Project instructions update automatically when the source document changes
Delete and recreate the Project from scratch with the new file
Remove the old style guide file from the Project and upload the new version, then update any instructions that referenced specific rules from the old guide
Create a new Project for the new style guide and keep the old one running
sections.explanation: Projects don't sync with external files automatically — you manage the content manually. The right approach is: delete the old file from the Project's knowledge base, upload the updated version, and review your instructions to see if any specific rules you referenced have changed. This keeps your Project current with minimal disruption.

sections.title: Workshop A — Quick Drill: Instruction Precision Test
sections.content:
This drill tests how precisely Claude follows written instructions — and teaches you to write tighter ones. Budget 8-10 minutes.

**Step 1 — Set up a test conversation (1 min)**
Open a fresh Claude conversation (not inside a Project yet). Ask:
```
Explain what a project management Gantt chart is and when to use one.
```
Note the response — length, format, tone.

**Step 2 — Give format instructions (2 min)**
In the same conversation:
```
Now answer the same question again, but follow these rules exactly:
- Maximum 80 words total
- No bullet points — only prose
- End with a one-sentence question that makes me think
- Do not use the word 'project'
```
Count the words. Did Claude follow all four rules? Note which rule(s) it broke, if any.

**Step 3 — Tighten the failure point (2 min)**
If Claude broke a rule, specifically address it:
```
You [describe what it got wrong]. Try again with all 4 rules satisfied.
```

**Step 4 — Test a trigger instruction (3 min)**
Start a new conversation. Imagine you're writing Project instructions. Test this trigger:
```
For this conversation, use this rule: whenever I start a message with 'QUICK:', give me a response of 3 sentences maximum.

QUICK: What's the difference between a goal and a KPI?
```
Did the trigger work? Try another:
```
QUICK: What's the most common mistake new managers make?
```

**Step 5 — Use AI to check your work (2 min)**
Ask Claude:
```
I'm about to add this instruction to a Claude Project:
'When I paste text, identify the document type and main purpose before doing anything else.'
Is this instruction clear enough, or could Claude interpret it in multiple ways?
Suggest a more precise version.
```

**Takeaway:** Precision in instructions is a skill. This drill shows you the difference between instructions that almost work and instructions that reliably work.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build It With AI: Your Master Project Instruction Set
sections.content:
You'll build a comprehensive, personalised instruction set for your primary Claude Project — one that will shape hundreds of future conversations. This takes 30-35 minutes and produces a real, working configuration.

**Step 1 — Audit your current situation (3 min)**
Open Claude.ai. Start a new conversation and type:
```
I'm building instructions for a persistent AI assistant that will help me with
[your primary use case — work tasks / learning / writing / job search / other].
Ask me 6 questions to understand my situation, goals, and preferences well enough
to write highly personalised instructions.
```
Answer each question in detail. The more specific your answers, the better the instructions.

**Step 2 — Generate a first draft of instructions (3 min)**
```
Based on my answers, write a complete Claude Project instruction set.
Include all 6 elements: who I am, what I'm working on, response format preferences,
things to avoid, domain knowledge to assume, and 2-3 task-type triggers.
Write it ready to paste directly into the Claude Project instruction field.
```

**Step 3 — Sharpen the "avoid" section (3 min)**
```
The 'Do not' section is the most practically useful part. Brainstorm 6 specific
Claude behaviours I should ban based on my preferences — things that would
actually waste my time or reduce output quality for my use case.
Be specific: 'Do not add a disclaimer at the end of writing tasks' is better
than 'Do not add unnecessary text'.
```
Pick the 3-4 best ones for your instruction set.

**Step 4 — Add smart triggers (3 min)**
```
Write 4 task-type triggers specific to what I actually do:
- When I [do X], you should [behave Y]
Base these on the tasks I described. Make the triggers recognisable from real inputs,
not hypothetical ones.
```

**Step 5 — Add an expertise calibration section (2 min)**
```
Write an 'Assume I know / Do explain' section based on my background.
List 4-5 things you should not explain (I already know them) and 3-4 types
of topics where you should explain from basics.
```

**Step 6 — Write a quality gate (2 min)**
```
Write a quality gate instruction — a self-check Claude should run before
delivering any substantial output. Base it on the 3 most common failures
for the type of work I described.
```

**Step 7 — Assemble the final instruction set (2 min)**
```
Assemble everything into one clean, final instruction set.
Format it clearly with section headers.
Target length: 300-400 words — detailed enough to be useful, short enough to be readable.
```

**Step 8 — Implement it (3 min)**
Copy the instruction set. Go to your primary Claude Project (or create one now). Paste the instructions into the instruction field. Save.

**Step 9 — Test with a real task (3 min)**
Start a conversation inside the Project. Give it a real task you have this week. Evaluate: does the response feel different from a standard conversation? Is it calibrated to your context?

**Step 10 — AI REVIEW (required) (3 min)**
Paste your instruction set back to Claude and ask:
```
Don't tell me what's good. Find 3 specific problems with these instructions:
- Any instruction that's ambiguous and could be interpreted two different ways
- Any important context about me that's missing
- Any instruction that will create annoying behaviour rather than helpful behaviour
Suggest fixes for each.
```
Fix at least one of the problems identified.

**Step 11 — Save a backup (1 min)**
Save the final instructions in a text file. Label it "Claude Project Instructions — [Date]." This backup means you can recreate the Project or share it with someone else.

**You've built:** A complete, personalised instruction set calibrated to your actual use case. This is the single highest-leverage configuration change available in Claude — and you've done it properly rather than with generic text.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI Review Round: Test Your Existing Instructions
sections.content:
If you already have a Claude Project, this workshop exposes weaknesses in your instructions. If you just created one in Workshop B, use those instructions. Either way, 10-15 minutes.

**Step 1 — Paste your current instructions for analysis (2 min)**
Open a new Claude conversation (outside any Project). Paste your current instruction set and say:
```
These are instructions for a Claude Project. Don't tell me what's good.
Only identify problems:
1. Instructions that are vague enough that Claude might interpret differently each time
2. Important context that's probably missing
3. Instructions that could accidentally produce worse outputs
4. Trigger phrases that might fire at the wrong time
```

**Step 2 — Stress test a specific trigger (3 min)**
Pick one of your trigger phrases. Ask Claude:
```
I have this trigger instruction: '[paste your trigger]'
Write 3 messages I might send where this trigger would fire incorrectly —
where the instruction would produce unhelpful behaviour.
```
This reveals false positives in your trigger logic.

**Step 3 — Find the missing context (3 min)**
```
Based on my instructions, what would Claude not know about me that could matter?
List 5 pieces of context that are probably missing.
```
Add the most important missing context to your actual instruction set.

**Step 4 — Test for instruction conflicts (2 min)**
```
Are there any instructions that contradict each other, or that together might
produce confused behaviour? For example, 'be concise' + 'always give 3 examples'
could conflict. List any conflicts you spot.
```

**Step 5 — Improve one thing now (3 min)**
Based on the analysis, choose the single most impactful improvement. Make the edit to your actual Project instructions.

**Reflect:** Instructions improve through use, not through getting them perfect upfront. This adversarial review process — deliberately hunting for failure modes — is how professional AI users maintain high-quality Project configurations.

sections.title: Workshop D — Real-World Application: Build a Specialist Project for a Real Need
sections.content:
Apply Projects to a specific, real challenge you currently face. You'll create a purpose-built Project with uploaded files — not a generic one, but one tailored to a concrete goal.

**Step 1 — Identify a specific real challenge (2 min)**
Choose from:
- You have a job interview coming up and want to prepare
- You're learning a new skill or subject and need a tutor
- You have a project proposal or report you need to write
- You manage a team and want help with communications and decisions
- You're planning a large event or trip
- You're working on a personal creative project

Be specific: not "writing help" but "help writing a grant application for my community arts project."

**Step 2 — Define the Project with Claude's help (5 min)**
Open Claude.ai. Ask:
```
I want to create a Claude Project for: [your specific challenge].
Help me design the ideal configuration by asking me what you'd need to know
to write instructions that would make this Project genuinely useful.
```
Answer Claude's questions.

**Step 3 — Write the instructions and gather files (5 min)**
Ask Claude to generate the instructions based on your answers. Then identify 2-3 files to upload:
- For job interview prep: your CV, the job description, the company's about page
- For learning: course notes, a textbook chapter, a syllabus
- For report writing: a previous report, a style guide, relevant data
- For team management: your team charter, a recent performance review, your management philosophy doc

**Step 4 — Create the Project and configure it (3 min)**
Create the Project in Claude.ai with the generated instructions. Upload the files. Name the Project specifically after the challenge: "Interview Prep — [Company Name]" or "Grant Application — [Project Name]."

**Step 5 — Run a real task (5 min)**
Start a conversation inside the Project and immediately give it the most important task you have for this challenge. Use the files. Evaluate the response.

**Step 6 — Refine and iterate (5 min)**
Based on the first response, adjust your instructions for anything that missed the mark. Add a specific instruction addressing what wasn't right. Run the task again.

**You've built:** A purpose-specific AI workspace for a real challenge — not a demo, but something that will actually save you time and improve your output on a task that matters.

sections.question: You're writing Claude Project instructions and want Claude to behave differently depending on what you send. Which instruction style is most effective?
options: 'Always be flexible and adapt to what I need'
'When I paste a document, summarise it first. When I ask a question, answer it directly. When I say REVIEW, give me critical feedback only.'
'Try to understand the context of my message before responding'
'Use your judgment about what type of response is most appropriate'
sections.explanation: Explicit trigger-based instructions ('When I [do X], you should [do Y]') are far more reliable than vague guidance about flexibility or judgment. Options A, C, and D tell Claude to use judgment — but Claude already does that by default. Option B gives Claude clear, recognisable signals that fire specific behaviours. The result is consistent, predictable responses rather than inconsistent outputs based on Claude's interpretation of what you might want.

sections.question: You use Claude Projects for work and Claude's memory feature is also active. A colleague asks why you don't have to re-explain your job every time you start a new conversation. What's the correct explanation?
options: Claude remembers all past conversations automatically

Projects store instructions that load at the start of each conversation in that Project, and Claude memory stores persistent facts across all conversations — together they eliminate most context-setting overhead
You must have paid for Claude Pro, which gives unlimited memory
Claude uses your email address to look up who you are
sections.explanation: Projects and memory work at different levels. Project instructions are manually written context that loads for every conversation within that specific Project. Claude memory is a separate system that learns and stores persistent facts across all conversations, not just Project ones. Together they cover both specific-context (Projects) and general identity (memory). Neither requires Pro for basic use, and neither works by looking up personal data — both are powered by context you've given Claude directly.

sections.question: Your Claude Project instructions say 'Keep responses to 3-5 bullet points.' You ask a complex question that genuinely requires a longer answer. What should you expect?
options: Claude will always follow the 3-5 bullet limit even if the answer suffers
Claude will completely ignore your instruction if it decides a longer response is better
Claude will generally follow the instruction but a direct in-conversation request ('this needs a fuller explanation') overrides the Project instruction for that response
The Project instruction is only a suggestion — Claude decides for itself
sections.explanation: Project instructions shape Claude's default behaviour but can be overridden in-conversation. Claude is designed to follow explicit in-conversation instructions over background Project instructions when there's a conflict. So 'Keep responses to 3-5 bullets' is a strong default, but if you say 'This question needs a full explanation — ignore the bullet limit,' Claude will respond appropriately. This makes Projects practical: you set sensible defaults that work for most interactions, and override when you genuinely need different behaviour.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 2-2.** You now have Claude Projects working for you — with custom instructions that automatically calibrate Claude to your context, uploaded files as a knowledge base, and a system for managing multiple Projects for different areas of your work. This is the single highest-leverage setup change you can make to get consistently better Claude output.
